body_text:
The Cayley-Hamilton Theorem. Every square matrix $A \in M_{n \times n}(F)$
satisfies its own characteristic polynomial: $\chi_A(A) = 0$.

*Proof Sketch*: Consider the adjugate matrix $B(t) = \operatorname{adj}(tI - A)$.
By the fundamental property of the classical adjugate:
$$ (tI - A) B(t) = \det(tI - A) I_n = \chi_A(t) I_n. $$
The entries of $B(t)$ are polynomials in $t$ of degree at most $n-1$,
so $B(t)$ can be expanded as a matrix polynomial:
$$ B(t) = B_{n-1} t^{n-1} + B_{n-2} t^{n-2} + \cdots + B_1 t + B_0 $$
with coefficient matrices $B_k \in M_{n \times n}(F)$.
If $\chi_A(t) = t^n + c_{n-1} t^{n-1} + \cdots + c_1 t + c_0$, equating
matrix coefficients of powers of $t$ in $(tI - A) B(t) = \chi_A(t) I_n$ gives:
$$ B_{n-1} = I, \quad B_{k-1} - A B_k = c_k I \quad (1 \leq k \leq n-1), \quad -A B_0 = c_0 I. $$
Multiplying each equation on the left by $A^k$ and summing telescopically yields:
$$ \chi_A(A) = A^n + c_{n-1} A^{n-1} + \cdots + c_1 A + c_0 I = 0. $$

The Cayley-Hamilton theorem establishes that $A^n$ can always be expressed
as a linear combination of lower powers $\{I, A, A^2, \dots, A^{n-1}\}$,
providing an invaluable computational tool for matrix powers, matrix exponentials,
and inverse computation.
